I am working on HSE LLM4Rec HW5 Week 5: From Ratings to Recommendations — Matrix Factorization.Files:

This is STEP 1 ONLY.
Do not modify any file.
Do not implement any TODO yet.
First, read all HW5 files completely and inspect the assignment requirements.
Then do the following:
1. Confirm the six actual student TODO(hw5) stubs in script.js:
   - predictRating
   - initializeFactors
   - trainMF
   - selectBestCheckpoint
   - recommendTopK
   - recallAtK
2. Confirm that the TODO(hw5) comment on splitByTimestamp() in data.js is not an unfinished student stub:
   - the function is already implemented;
   - data.js is professor-provided and must not be modified.
3. Identify all professor-provided scaffolding that must stay unchanged, especially:
   - initTf
   - computeRMSEFor
   - computeBaselineRMSE
   - formatting helpers
   - DOM renderers
   - hyperparameter reader
   - pipeline wrapper
   - test harness
   - data.js
   - index.html
   - style.css
4. Run the app correctly over HTTP, not file://, because data.js uses fetch().
5. Confirm TensorFlow.js loads successfully and report the actual backend:
   - webgl or
   - cpu
6. Click Run tests in the browser and record the exact baseline result.
   The README says the untouched starter should show:
   - Passed: 4
   - Failed: 0
   - Pending: 7
   Do not copy these numbers from the README. Actually run the browser tests and verify them.
7. Inspect all 11 self-checks and explain exactly what each test verifies.
8. Confirm dataset facts from the actual files:
   - number of ratings
   - number of movies
   - number of users
   - max user id
   - max movie id
   - matrix shape
   - rating range
   - presence of timestamps
   - genre parsing layout
9. Verify the genre alignment in data.js:
   - field 5 is the legacy unknown flag;
   - real genres are fields 6..23;
   - confirm slice(6, 24) correctly maps to the 18 genre names.
10. Inspect splitByTimestamp() and verify the exact split logic:
    - per user
    - ascending timestamp
    - movieId tie-break
    - floor(0.8*n) train
    - floor(0.1*n) validation
    - remainder test
    - users with fewer than 5 ratings are excluded and recorded
11. Record the actual split sizes on the full MovieLens dataset:
    - train count
    - validation count
    - test count
    - number of excluded users
12. Trace the full current pipeline:
    u.data/u.item
    → parsing
    → rating matrix
    → chronological split
    → training mean baseline
    → factor initialization
    → MF training
    → validation RMSE checkpoint selection
    → test RMSE
    → Top-10 recommendation
    → Recall@10
    Show exactly where the current starter stops because of the TODO stubs.
13. Inspect the precise prediction contract:
    r_hat(u,i) = globalMean + p_u · q_i
    then clamp to [1,5].
    Confirm:
    - 16 latent dimensions in the default pipeline;
    - raw user/movie IDs index factor rows;
    - unknown/out-of-range IDs fall back to globalMean;
    - uninitialized model returns 0 where specified.
14. Inspect the training requirements:
    - TensorFlow.js batched tensor operations
    - no handwritten per-rating training loop
    - Adam or SGD
    - squared-error objective
    - L2 regularization
    - tf.tidy
    - dispose tensors/variables correctly
    - one history row per epoch
15. Inspect checkpoint selection:
    - smallest validation RMSE wins
    - ties must choose the earliest epoch
16. Inspect recommendation requirements:
    - score all eligible candidate movies
    - use tensor scoring (matMul / tf.topk)
    - exclude movies rated by the user in train or validation
    - test-rated movies remain eligible
    - exclude IDs absent from the movies list
    - Top-K sorted descending
17. Inspect Recall@10 requirements:
    - relevant = test rating >= 4.0
    - global candidate pool = movie IDs appearing in training
    - per-user recall = hits / eligible relevant candidate movies
    - overall recall = mean over evaluable users
    - report unseen relevant movie IDs
    - report users without an eligible relevant test movie
18. Identify the evidence we must collect later for c2:
    - real baseline 4/0/7
    - final 11/0/0
    - actual TensorFlow.js backend
    - validation RMSE at selected checkpoint
    - MF test RMSE
    - baseline test RMSE
    - at least one independently hand-checked RMSE or prediction
    - two Top-10 lists
    - proof that train/val items are excluded
    - Recall@10
    - unseen-item exclusion count
    - users-without-relevant count
    - one re-run / cross-check
    - file integrity showing only script.js changed later
19. Identify the evidence we must collect later for c1, especially the mandatory question:
    Familiar Choices vs. New Discoveries
    Plan how to compare two users using:
    - their past highly rated movies
    - past genres
    - Top-10 recommended titles
    - recommended genres
    - familiar vs novel items
    - an explicit streaming-platform conclusion
    Do not reduce this to RMSE or Recall@10.
    We must explicitly answer what the recommendation lists are worth to the platform, e.g.:
    - retention through familiar choices,
    - catalog discovery,
    - engagement,
    - avoiding over-narrow personalization,
    - or another justified business/platform axis.
20. Check the assignment for any ambiguity, inconsistency, or grading risk and flag it before implementation.
Return the result under these sections:
- Baseline summary
- Files inspected
- Six real TODO functions
- Provided scaffolding
- Data.js TODO-comment clarification

1: /**
2:  * week5/script.js — Matrix Factorization with TensorFlow.js (HW5).
3:  *
4:  * This is a plain (classic) script, NOT an ES module. `index.html` loads the
5:  * TensorFlow.js runtime from a CDN before this file, exposing the global `tf`:
6:  *
7:  *   <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@tensorflow/tfjs@4.22.0/dist/tf.min.js"></script>
8:  *   <script src="data.js"></script>
9:  *   <script src="script.js"></script>
10:  *
11:  * `week5/data.js` (loaded before this file) exposes the MovieLens 100k data
12:  * layer as globals: `movies`, `ratings`, `numUsers`, `numMovies`,
13:  * `ratingMatrix`, `SPLIT_EXCLUSIONS`, `loadData()` and `splitByTimestamp()`.
14:  * This file reads those globals, renders a dataset / split summary, and wires
15:  * the page controls. The factorization itself is built on `tf.Variable`s and
16:  * tensor ops so it can run on the WebGL (GPU) backend.
17:  *
18:  * BACKEND: `initTf()` prefers WebGL, falls back to CPU, and writes the chosen
19:  * backend into `#tf-status`. If the CDN did not load (`typeof tf ===
20:  * 'undefined'`) the page shows a clear message and stops instead of throwing.
21:  *
22:  * WHAT YOU MUST IMPLEMENT (`TODO(hw5)` — each stub throws until you write it):
23:  *   1. `predictRating`        — scalar gather + dot + globalMean, clamp [1, 5].
24:  *   2. `initializeFactors`    — two `tf.Variable`s + the global mean.
25:  *   3. `trainMF`              — batched tensor training loop with L2 / Adam.
26:  *   4. `selectBestCheckpoint` — earliest entry with the smallest val RMSE.
27:  *   5. `recommendTopK`        — `matMul` + `tf.topk`, exclude train/val items.
28:  *   6. `recallAtK`            — Recall@K against relevant (>= 4.0) test items.
29:  *
30:  * PROVIDED for you (scaffolding): `initTf`, the shared metric helpers
31:  * (`computeRMSEFor`, `computeBaselineRMSE`), formatting helpers, every DOM
32:  * renderer, the hyper-parameter reader, the training pipeline wrapper, and the
33:  * automated test harness. Leave the provided code as-is and implement only the
34:  * six stubs.
35:  *
36:  * The harness reports unimplemented stubs as PENDING rather than FAIL, so the
37:  * page stays usable before and after the assignment is done.
38:  *
39:  * @module week5/script
40:  */
41: 
42: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
43: // Typedefs
44: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
45: 
46: /**
47:  * @typedef {Object} Movie
48:  * @property {number} id
49:  * @property {string} title
50:  * @property {string[]} genres
51:  */
52: 
53: /**
54:  * @typedef {Object} Rating
55:  * @property {number} userId
56:  * @property {number} movieId
57:  * @property {number} rating
58:  * @property {number} timestamp
59:  */
60: 
61: /**
62:  * @typedef {Object} Model
63:  * @property {tf.Variable} userFactors Dense factor matrix `[numUsers + 1, F]`,
64:  *   row index = raw `userId`.
65:  * @property {tf.Variable} itemFactors Dense factor matrix `[maxMovieId + 1, F]`,
66:  *   row index = raw `movieId`.
67:  * @property {number} globalMean       Mean rating of the training set.
68:  */
69: 
70: /**
71:  * @typedef {Object} HistoryRow
72:  * @property {number} epoch
73:  * @property {number} trainRMSE
74:  * @property {number} valRMSE
75:  */
76: 
77: /**
78:  * @typedef {Object} TrainOptions
79:  * @property {number} epochs    Number of full passes over the training set.
80:  * @property {number} lr        Learning rate.
81:  * @property {number} reg       L2 regularization strength.
82:  * @property {number} batchSize Mini-batch size.
83:  */
84: 
85: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
86: // State
87: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
88: 
89: /** Number of latent factors used by the default pipeline. */
90: const NUM_FACTORS = 16;
91: 
92: /** Training split (80% of each user's ratings, oldest first). */
93: let trainSet = [];
94: 
95: /** Validation split (10% of each user's ratings). */
96: let valSet = [];
97: 
98: /** Test split (10% of each user's ratings, newest). */
99: let testSet = [];
100: 
101: /**
102:  * The fitted factorization, or `null` before `initializeFactors` runs.
103:  *
104:  * @type {Model|null}
105:  */
106: let model = null;
107: 
108: /**
109:  * Metric history produced by `trainMF`.
110:  *
111:  * @type {HistoryRow[]}
112:  */
113: let trainingHistory = [];
114: 
115: /**
116:  * The history entry returned by `selectBestCheckpoint`, or `null`.
117:  *
118:  * @type {HistoryRow|null}
119:  */
120: let bestCheckpoint = null;
121: 
122: /** Name of the TensorFlow.js backend selected by `initTf` (`"webgl"` / `"cpu"`). */
123: let tfBackend = null;
124: 
125: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
126: // TensorFlow.js bootstrap (provided)
127: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
128: 
129: /**
130:  * Select the fastest available TensorFlow.js backend and report it.
131:  *
132:  * Tries WebGL (GPU) first and falls back to the pure-JS CPU backend. Writes
133:  * `backend: <name>` into `#tf-status` when that element exists. If the CDN
134:  * failed, `tf` is undefined: this renders a readable message and returns
135:  * `null` instead of letting the page throw an uncaught `ReferenceError`.
136:  *
137:  * @returns {Promise<string|null>} the selected backend, or `null` when TF.js is missing.
138:  */
139: async function initTf() {
140:   const statusEl = document.getElementById("tf-status");
141:   if (typeof tf === "undefined") {
142:     const message =
143:       "TensorFlow.js failed to load. Check your network connection (the CDN script) and reload the page.";
144:     if (statusEl) {
145:       statusEl.textContent = message;
146:       statusEl.className = "error";
147:     } else if (document.body) {
148:       const banner = document.createElement("p");
149:       banner.className = "error";
150:       banner.textContent = message;
151:       document.body.insertBefore(banner, document.body.firstChild);
152:     }
153:     return null;
154:   }
155: 
156:   try {
157:     await tf.setBackend("webgl");
158:   } catch (error) {
159:     await tf.setBackend("cpu");
160:   }
161:   await tf.ready();
162: 
163:   tfBackend = tf.getBackend();
164:   if (statusEl) statusEl.textContent = `TensorFlow.js backend: ${tfBackend}`;
165:   return tfBackend;
166: }
167: 
168: /**
169:  * True when `candidate` is a TF.js factor model (dense `tf.Variable` rows).
170:  *
171:  * Used to route `computeRMSEFor` through the batched tensor path and to keep
172:  * the fixture-based tests independent of how the model was produced.
173:  *
174:  * @param {*} candidate
175:  * @returns {boolean}
176:  */
177: function isTfModel(candidate) {
178:   return (
179:     !!candidate &&
180:     !!candidate.userFactors &&
181:     typeof candidate.userFactors.dataSync === "function" &&
182:     !!candidate.itemFactors &&
183:     typeof candidate.itemFactors.dataSync === "function"
184:   );
185: }
186: 
187: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
188: // Formatting helpers (provided)
189: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
190: 
191: /**
192:  * Format a number to a fixed number of decimals. Non-finite and missing values
193:  * render as an em dash so the tables never show `NaN` or `undefined`.
194:  *
195:  * @param {number|null|undefined} x
196:  * @param {number} [d=4] decimal places
197:  * @returns {string}
198:  */
199: function fmt(x, d = 4) {
200:   if (x === null || x === undefined) return "\u2014";
201:   const n = Number(x);
202:   if (!Number.isFinite(n)) return "\u2014";
203:   return n.toFixed(d);
204: }
205: 
206: /**
207:  * Look up a movie title by id, with a readable fallback for unknown ids.
208:  *
209:  * @param {number|string} id
210:  * @returns {string}
211:  */
212: function movieTitle(id) {
213:   const numericId = Number(id);
214:   const movie = movies.find((m) => m.id === numericId);
215:   return movie ? movie.title : `Movie #${id}`;
216: }
217: 
218: /**
219:  * Escape text before inserting it into HTML.
220:  *
221:  * @param {string} text
222:  * @returns {string}
223:  */
224: function escapeHtml(text) {
225:   return String(text)
226:     .replace(/&/g, "&")
227:     .replace(/</g, "<")
228:     .replace(/>/g, ">")
229:     .replace(/"/g, """)
230:     .replace(/'/g, "'");
231: }
232: 
233: /**
234:  * Clamp a number into the inclusive range `[lo, hi]`.
235:  *
236:  * @param {number} value
237:  * @param {number} lo
238:  * @param {number} hi
239:  * @returns {number}
240:  */
241: function clamp(value, lo, hi) {
242:   return Math.min(hi, Math.max(lo, value));
243: }
244: 
245: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
246: // Shared metric helpers (provided)
247: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
248: 
249: /**
250:  * Root-mean-square error of the current model over a split.
251:  *
252:  * Provided so that `trainMF` and the test harness share one implementation.
253:  *
254:  * When `model` holds TF.js variables this builds the index tensors ONCE, uses
255:  * `tf.gather` + element-wise multiply to score every rating in a single batch,
256:  * and clamps to `[1, 5]` — the same contract as `predictRating`, but fast
257:  * enough to call every epoch. Out-of-range ids fall back to `globalMean`, and
258:  * the whole computation runs inside `tf.tidy` so the intermediate tensors are
259:  * released automatically.
260:  *
261:  * When no TF.js model is available it falls back to the scalar
262:  * `predictRating` loop. That path returns `NaN` instead of throwing while
263:  * `predictRating` is still a `TODO(hw5)` stub, so the helper never crashes the
264:  * page or the harness.
265:  *
266:  * @param {Rating[]} split
267:  * @returns {number} `0` for an empty split; `NaN` if the scalar path throws.
268:  */
269: function computeRMSEFor(split) {
270:   if (!split || split.length === 0) return 0;
271: 
272:   if (isTfModel(model)) {
273:     return tf.tidy(() => {
274:       const n = split.length;
275:       const uRows = model.userFactors.shape[0];
276:       const iRows = model.itemFactors.shape[0];
277:       const userIds = new Int32Array(n);
278:       const movieIds = new Int32Array(n);
279:       const actual = new Float32Array(n);
280:       const valid = new Float32Array(n);
281: 
282:       for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) {
283:         const r = split[k];
284:         userIds[k] = r.userId;
285:         movieIds[k] = r.movieId;
286:         actual[k] = r.rating;
287:         const uOk = r.userId >= 0 && r.userId < uRows;
288:         const iOk = r.movieId >= 0 && r.movieId < iRows;
289:         valid[k] = uOk && iOk ? 1 : 0;
290:       }
291: 
292:       const uIdx = tf.clipByValue(tf.tensor1d(userIds, "int32"), 0, Math.max(0, uRows - 1));
293:       const iIdx = tf.clipByValue(tf.tensor1d(movieIds, "int32"), 0, Math.max(0, iRows - 1));
294:       const u = tf.gather(model.userFactors, uIdx);
295:       const i = tf.gather(model.itemFactors, iIdx);
296:       const dot = tf.sum(tf.mul(u, i), 1);
297:       const mask = tf.tensor1d(valid, "float32");
298:       const pred = tf.clipByValue(dot.mul(mask).add(model.globalMean), 1, 5);
299:       const diff = pred.sub(tf.tensor1d(actual, "float32"));
300:       return Math.sqrt(tf.mean(diff.square()).dataSync()[0]);
301:     });
302:   }
303: 
304:   let sum = 0;
305:   try {
306:     for (const r of split) {
307:       const diff = predictRating(r.userId, r.movieId) - r.rating;
308:       sum += diff * diff;
309:     }
310:   } catch (error) {
311:     return Number.NaN;
312:   }
313:   return Math.sqrt(sum / split.length);
314: }
315: 
316: /**
317:  * Baseline RMSE: predict the training-set mean rating for every pair and
318:  * measure the error on `split`. This is the number your factorization must beat.
319:  *
320:  * @param {Rating[]} split
321:  * @returns {number} `0` for an empty split (never divides by zero).
322:  */
323: function computeBaselineRMSE(split) {
324:   if (!split || split.length === 0) return 0;
325:   const mean = trainSet.length
326:     ? trainSet.reduce((acc, r) => acc + r.rating, 0) / trainSet.length
327:     : 0;
328:   let sum = 0;
329:   for (const r of split) {
330:     const diff = mean - r.rating;
331:     sum += diff * diff;
332:   }
333:   return Math.sqrt(sum / split.length);
334: }
335: 
336: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
337: // Student stubs (TODO(hw5))
338: //
339: // Each stub below throws until you implement it. Fill in the body, keep the
340: // signature, and update the JSDoc contract notes if your design differs.
341: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
342: 
343: /**
344:  * Predict the rating a user would give a movie (scalar).
345:  *
346:  * TODO(hw5): implement the prediction with TensorFlow.js. The model stores the
347:  * factors as two dense `tf.Variable`s:
348:  *   - `model.userFactors` shape `[numUsers + 1, F]`, row index = `userId`
349:  *   - `model.itemFactors` shape `[maxMovieId + 1, F]`, row index = `movieId`
350:  *
351:  * Suggested TF.js path (wrap it in `tf.tidy` and pull out a JS number):
352:  * ```js
353:  * const f = model.userFactors.shape[1];
354:  * return tf.tidy(() => {
355:  *   const u = model.userFactors.slice([userId, 0], [1, f]); // [1, F]
356:  *   const i = model.itemFactors.slice([movieId, 0], [1, f]); // [1, F]
357:  *   const dot = u.mul(i).sum().dataSync()[0];                // scalar
358:  *   return clamp(model.globalMean + dot, 1, 5);
359:  * });
360:  * ```
361:  * `dataSync()` copies the value to the CPU as a plain number, which survives
362:  * `tf.tidy` (the tensors do not). Keep this function scalar: `computeRMSEFor`
363:  * uses its own batched tensor path, and the harness calls it once per pair.
364:  *
365:  * Contract:
366:  *  - Return `model.globalMean` when the user or movie row is out of range
367:  *    (an id that has no allocated factor row). Never throw for an unknown id.
368:  *  - Return `0` when the model is not initialized (`model === null`) so callers
369:  *    can guard cheaply.
370:  *  - The result is clamped to `[1, 5]`.
371:  *
372:  * @param {number} userId
373:  * @param {number} movieId
374:  * @returns {number} predicted rating in `[1, 5]`
375:  */
376: function predictRating(userId, movieId) {
377:   // TODO(hw5): gather the two factor rows, take their dot product, add
378:   // globalMean and clamp the result to [1, 5].
379:   throw new Error("TODO(hw5): predictRating is not implemented yet.");
380: }
381: 
382: /**
383:  * Allocate the latent factor variables and the global mean.
384:  *
385:  * TODO(hw5): compute `globalMean` as the mean rating over `train`
386:  * (`0` for an empty training set), then create the two dense variables:
387:  * ```js
388:  * const maxMovieId = movies.reduce((m, x) => Math.max(m, x.id), 0);
389:  * model = {
390:  *   userFactors: tf.variable(tf.randomNormal([numUsers + 1, numFactors], 0, 0.05)),
391:  *   itemFactors: tf.variable(tf.randomNormal([maxMovieId + 1, numFactors], 0, 0.05)),
392:  *   globalMean,
393:  * };
394:  * ```
395:  * `tf.randomNormal(shape, mean, std)` draws small values — use a small std
396:  * (e.g. `0.05`) so training starts near the global mean. `tf.variable` wraps a
397:  * tensor so the optimizer can update it in place. Store the result on the
398:  * module-level `model` object and return it.
399:  *
400:  * Contract:
401:  *  - `numFactors` defaults to the module-level `NUM_FACTORS`.
402:  *  - If a previous `model` exists, dispose its variables (`tf.dispose`) before
403:  *    replacing it so repeated "Train" clicks do not leak GPU memory.
404:  *  - Return the `model` object.
405:  *
406:  * @param {Rating[]} train
407:  * @param {number} [numFactors=NUM_FACTORS]
408:  * @returns {Model}
409:  */
410: function initializeFactors(train, numFactors = NUM_FACTORS) {
411:   // TODO(hw5): compute globalMean, create the two tf.Variables, assign to model.
412:   throw new Error("TODO(hw5): initializeFactors is not implemented yet.");
413: }
414: 
415: /**
416:  * Train the factorization with batched gradient descent.
417:  *
418:  * TODO(hw5): run a mini-batch loop over `train` using the TF.js optimizer.
419:  * Score each batch with tensor ops (never one `tf` call per rating) and let the
420:  * optimizer update both variables in place:
421:  * ```js
422:  * const optimizer = tf.train.adam(lr);
423:  * for (let epoch = 1; epoch <= epochs; epoch++) {
424:  *   for (const batch of batches) {
425:  *     optimizer.minimize(() => tf.tidy(() => {
426:  *       const u = tf.gather(model.userFactors, batch.userIdx);
427:  *       const i = tf.gather(model.itemFactors, batch.itemIdx);
428:  *       const pred = tf.sum(u.mul(i), 1).add(model.globalMean);
429:  *       const mse = tf.losses.meanSquaredError(batch.targets, pred);
430:  *       const l2 = model.userFactors.square().sum()
431:  *         .add(model.itemFactors.square().sum()).mul(reg);
432:  *       return mse.add(l2);
433:  *     }), false, [model.userFactors, model.itemFactors]).dispose();
434:  *   }
435:  *   trainingHistory.push({
436:  *     epoch,
437:  *     trainRMSE: computeRMSEFor(train),
438:  *     valRMSE: computeRMSEFor(val),
439:  *   });
440:  * }
441:  * return trainingHistory;
442:  * ```
443:  * Key TF.js APIs to use: `tf.train.adam(lr)` (or `tf.train.sgd`),
444:  * `optimizer.minimize(fn, returnCost, varList)`, `tf.gather`,
445:  * `tf.losses.meanSquaredError`, and `tf.tidy` for per-batch intermediates.
446:  * `minimize` returns a scalar loss tensor — dispose it (or use `tf.tidy`) so
447:  * the loop does not accumulate tensors.
448:  *
449:  * Contract:
450:  *  - `opts = { epochs, lr, reg, batchSize }`. Use mini-batches of `batchSize`
451:  *    (or full-batch when `batchSize >= train.length`).
452:  *  - Update `model` in place. Do NOT reallocate it.

454:  *    and return it: `{ epoch, trainRMSE: computeRMSEFor(train),

456:  *  - Shuffling the batch order each epoch is allowed and usually helps.
457:  *  - Guard `train.length === 0` by returning an empty history.
458:  *
459:  * @param {Rating[]} train

848: /**
849:  * Build a TF.js factor model from sparse score maps.
850:  *
851:  * `userScores[id]` / `itemScores[id]` may be a number (written into factor 0,
852:  * so the dot product is just the product) or an array (written across factors).
853:  * Rows are dense and indexed by raw id, exactly like the real model, so the
854:  * recommendation / recall fixtures exercise the same tensor path as training.
855:  *
856:  * @param {Object<number, number|number[]>} userScores
857:  * @param {Object<number, number|number[]>} itemScores
858:  * @param {number} [globalMean=0]
859:  * @returns {Model}
860:  */
861: function fixtureModel(userScores, itemScores, globalMean = 0) {
862:   const F = NUM_FACTORS;
863:   const userIds = Object.keys(userScores).map(Number);
864:   const itemIds = Object.keys(itemScores).map(Number);
865: 
866:   // A number goes into factor 0 (so the dot product is the product); an array
867:   // is copied across the first factors.
868:   const rowsFor = (value) => {
869:     if (Array.isArray(value) || ArrayBuffer.isView(value)) return Array.from(value);
870:     const row = new Array(F).fill(0);
871:     row[0] = Number(value);
872:     return row;
873:   };
874: 
875:   const maxUser = Math.max(numUsers, ...userIds);
876:   const maxMovieFromMovies = movies.reduce((m, x) => Math.max(m, x.id), 0);
877:   const maxItem = Math.max(maxMovieFromMovies, ...itemIds);
878: 
879:   const uData = new Float32Array((maxUser + 1) * F);
880:   for (const id of userIds) {
881:     const row = rowsFor(userScores[id]);
882:     for (let f = 0; f < Math.min(F, row.length); f++) uData[id * F + f] = row[f];
883:   }
884:   const iData = new Float32Array((maxItem + 1) * F);
885:   for (const id of itemIds) {
886:     const row = rowsFor(itemScores[id]);
887:     for (let f = 0; f < Math.min(F, row.length); f++) iData[id * F + f] = row[f];
888:   }
889: 
890:   return {
891:     userFactors: tf.variable(tf.tensor2d(uData, [maxUser + 1, F])),
892:     itemFactors: tf.variable(tf.tensor2d(iData, [maxItem + 1, F])),
893:     globalMean,
894:   };
895: }

931:  * @param {{movies?: Movie[], train?: Rating[], val?: Rating[], test?: Rating[], model?: Model|null, history?: HistoryRow[]}} fixture
932:  * @param {() => any} fn
933:  * @returns {any}
934:  */
935: function withFixture(fixture, fn) {
936:   const saved = { movies, trainSet, valSet, testSet, model, trainingHistory };
937:   try {
938:     movies = fixture.movies !== undefined ? fixture.movies : movies;
939:     trainSet = fixture.train || [];
940:     valSet = fixture.val || [];
941:     testSet = fixture.test || [];
942:     model = fixture.model !== undefined ? fixture.model : null;
943:     trainingHistory = fixture.history || [];
944:     return fn();
945:   } finally {
946:     movies = saved.movies;
947:     trainSet = saved.trainSet;
948:     valSet = saved.valSet;
949:     testSet = saved.testSet;
950:     model = saved.model;
951:     trainingHistory = saved.trainingHistory;

/**
 * week5/script.js — Matrix Factorization with TensorFlow.js (HW5).
 *
 * This is a plain (classic) script, NOT an ES module. `index.html` loads the
 * TensorFlow.js runtime from a CDN before this file, exposing the global `tf`:
 *
 *   <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@tensorflow/tfjs@4.22.0/dist/tf.min.js"></script>
 *   <script src="data.js"></script>
 *   <script src="script.js"></script>
 *
 * `week5/data.js` (loaded before this file) exposes the MovieLens 100k data
 * layer as globals: `movies`, `ratings`, `numUsers`, `numMovies`,
 * `ratingMatrix`, `SPLIT_EXCLUSIONS`, `loadData()` and `splitByTimestamp()`.
 * This file reads those globals, renders a dataset / split summary, and wires
 * the page controls. The factorization itself is built on `tf.Variable`s and
 * tensor ops so it can run on the WebGL (GPU) backend.
 *
 * BACKEND: `initTf()` prefers WebGL, falls back to CPU, and writes the chosen

1: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
2: // week5/data.js — MovieLens 100k data layer (classic <script>, no modules)
3: //
4: // Loads u.item (movies) and u.data (ratings), builds a sparse-friendly
5: // rating matrix, and splits every user's ratings chronologically 80/10/10.
6: //
7: // Genre alignment note (fixes the Week-2 off-by-one):
8: //   A u.item row has 24 '|'-separated fields:
9: //     0 id | 1 title | 2 release | 3 video | 4 url | 5 unknown |
10: //     6 Action | 7 Adventure | ... | 23 Western
11: //   Field index 5 is the legacy 19th genre flag "unknown", NOT the first real
12: //   genre. The 18 real flags therefore live at indices 6..23, so we read them
13: //   with fields.slice(6, 24) and pair them with the 18-name `genreNames`
14: //   list below. (The earlier fields.slice(5, 24) + 18 names pairing was off
15: //   by one.)
16: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
17: 
18: // Global variables for storing movie and rating data
19: let movies = [];          // [{ id, title, genres: string[] }]
20: let ratings = [];         // [{ userId, movieId, rating, timestamp }]
21: 
22: // Collaborative filtering structures (populated by buildRatingMatrix)
23: let numUsers = 0;         // highest user id found in u.data
24: let numMovies = 0;        // number of parsed movies
25: let ratingMatrix = null;  // (numUsers + 1) x (maxMovieId + 1); 0 = unobserved
26: 
27: // Genre names for the 18 real flags (u.item field indices 6..23)
28: const genreNames = [
29:     "Action", "Adventure", "Animation", "Children's", "Comedy",
30:     "Crime", "Documentary", "Drama", "Fantasy", "Film-Noir",
31:     "Horror", "Musical", "Mystery", "Romance", "Sci-Fi",
32:     "Thriller", "War", "Western"
33: ];
34: 
35: // Users skipped while splitting (e.g. too few ratings), collected by
36: // splitByTimestamp() for reporting.
37: let SPLIT_EXCLUSIONS = [];
38: 
39: // Primary function to load data from files
40: async function loadData() {
41:     try {
42:         // Load and parse movie data
43:         const moviesResponse = await fetch('u.item');
44:         if (!moviesResponse.ok) {
45:             throw new Error(`Failed to load movie data: ${moviesResponse.status}`);
46:         }
47:         const moviesText = await moviesResponse.text();
48:         parseItemData(moviesText);
49: 
50:         // Load and parse rating data
51:         const ratingsResponse = await fetch('u.data');
52:         if (!ratingsResponse.ok) {
53:             throw new Error(`Failed to load rating data: ${ratingsResponse.status}`);
54:         }
55:         const ratingsText = await ratingsResponse.text();
56:         parseRatingData(ratingsText);
57: 
58:         // Derive matrix dimensions, then build the rating matrix
59:         numUsers = ratings.reduce((max, r) => Math.max(max, r.userId), 0);
60:         numMovies = movies.length;
61:         buildRatingMatrix();
62:     } catch (error) {
63:         console.error('Error loading data:', error);
64:         const errorTarget = document.getElementById('result');
65:         if (errorTarget) {
66:             errorTarget.textContent =
67:                 `Error: ${error.message}. Please make sure u.item and u.data are in the correct location.`;
68:             errorTarget.className = 'error';
69:         }
70:         throw error; // Re-throw so the page script can handle the error
71:     }
72: }
73: 
74: // Parse movie data from u.item format: "id|title|release|video|url|g0|...|g18"
75: // genreNames has 18 entries, matched against the real flags at indices 6..23.
76: function parseItemData(text) {
77:     const lines = text.split('\n');
78: 
79:     for (const line of lines) {
80:         if (line.trim() === '') continue;
81: 
82:         const fields = line.split('|');
83:         if (fields.length < 24) continue; // Skip malformed rows
84: 
85:         const id = parseInt(fields[0]);
86:         const title = fields[1];
87: 
88:         // Read the 18 real genre flags (index 5 is the 'unknown' placeholder)
89:         const genreValues = fields.slice(6, 24).map(value => parseInt(value));
90:         const genres = genreNames.filter((_, index) => genreValues[index] === 1);
91: 
92:         movies.push({ id, title, genres });
93:     }
94: }
95: 
96: // Parse rating data from u.data format: "userId\tmovieId\trating\ttimestamp"
97: function parseRatingData(text) {
98:     const lines = text.split('\n');
99: 
100:     for (const line of lines) {
101:         if (line.trim() === '') continue;
102: 
103:         const fields = line.split('\t');
104:         if (fields.length < 4) continue; // Skip malformed rows
105: 
106:         const userId = parseInt(fields[0]);
107:         const movieId = parseInt(fields[1]);
108:         const rating = parseFloat(fields[2]);
109:         const timestamp = parseInt(fields[3]);
110: 
111:         ratings.push({ userId, movieId, rating, timestamp });
112:     }
113: }
114: 
115: // Build the sparse-friendly rating matrix.
116: // Shape: (numUsers + 1) x (maxMovieId + 1), indexed by raw ids, so that
117: //   ratingMatrix[userId][movieId] === rating
118: // and an unobserved pair is 0. MovieLens ratings are 1-5, so 0 is unambiguous.
119: function buildRatingMatrix() {
120:     const maxMovieId = movies.reduce((max, m) => Math.max(max, m.id), 0);
121: 
122:     ratingMatrix = [];
123:     for (let u = 0; u <= numUsers; u++) {
124:         ratingMatrix.push(new Array(maxMovieId + 1).fill(0));
125:     }
126: 
127:     for (const r of ratings) {
128:         if (r.userId <= numUsers && r.movieId <= maxMovieId) {
129:             ratingMatrix[r.userId][r.movieId] = r.rating;
130:         }
131:     }
132: }
133: 
134: // TODO(hw5): split EACH user's ratings by ascending timestamp into 80/10/10.
135: // Returns { train, val, test }, each an array of the same
136: // { userId, movieId, rating, timestamp } objects.
137: //
138: // Rules:
139: //   - counts are deterministic: nTrain = floor(0.8 * n), nVal = floor(0.1 * n),
140: //     nTest = n - nTrain - nVal (the remainder)
141: //   - users with fewer than 5 ratings are skipped and recorded in
142: //     SPLIT_EXCLUSIONS
143: //   - timestamp ties are broken by movieId so the split is deterministic
144: function splitByTimestamp() {
145:     const MIN_RATINGS = 5;
146: 
147:     const byUser = new Map();
148:     for (const r of ratings) {
149:         if (!byUser.has(r.userId)) byUser.set(r.userId, []);
150:         byUser.get(r.userId).push(r);
151:     }
152: 
153:     const train = [];
154:     const val = [];
155:     const test = [];
156: 
157:     SPLIT_EXCLUSIONS = [];
158: 
159:     for (const [userId, userRatings] of byUser) {
160:         const n = userRatings.length;
161:         if (n < MIN_RATINGS) {
162:             SPLIT_EXCLUSIONS.push({
163:                 userId,
164:                 count: n,
165:                 reason: `fewer than ${MIN_RATINGS} ratings`
166:             });
167:             continue;
168:         }
169: 
170:         const sorted = userRatings.slice().sort((a, b) =>
171:             a.timestamp - b.timestamp || a.movieId - b.movieId
172:         );
173: 
174:         const nTrain = Math.floor(0.8 * n);
175:         const nVal = Math.floor(0.1 * n);
176: 
177:         for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
178:             if (i < nTrain) train.push(sorted[i]);
179:             else if (i < nTrain + nVal) val.push(sorted[i]);
180:             else test.push(sorted[i]);
181:         }
182:     }
183: 
184:     return { train, val, test };
185: }

(End of file - total 185 lines)

1: # HW5 — From Ratings to Recommendations (Matrix Factorization)
2: 
3: **Course**: LLM4Rec, HSE University
4: **Instructor**: Seungmin Jin (sedzhin@hse.ru)
5: **Repository**: https://github.com/dryjins/RecSys-LLMs/tree/main/week5
6: **Task type**: Assignment (individual)
7: 
8: ---
9: 
10: ## 1. Learning goals
11: 
12: By the end of this assignment you should be able to:
13: 
14: - Turn a sparse rating log into a **user–movie rating matrix** and explain why an
15:   unobserved rating is **missing data, not a zero**.
16: - Split ratings **per user, by timestamp**, into an **80% train / 10% validation /
17:   10% test** protocol that mimics "predict the future from the past".
18: - Implement **matrix factorization** with **16-dimensional** user and movie
19:   vectors and a **dot-product** prediction rule.
20: - Train the factors with **batched tensor operations in TensorFlow.js**, using

# Skill: pptx

# PPTX creation, editing, and analysis

If this session offers a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill, and the user has neither asked for a PowerPoint/.pptx file nor supplied a .pptx/.potx file to edit, fill in, or convert, build the deck with that type or skill instead. A .pptx/.potx file given only as source material or as an example for a new deck ("make another deck like this one") does not count as supplied: read it with this skill, then build the new deck with that type or skill. This skill remains the right tool for producing .pptx files and for reading, editing, templating, or converting existing .pptx/.potx files.

A `.pptx` is a ZIP archive of XML files. Choose your approach by task:

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** a new deck | Write a `pptxgenjs` script — see gotchas below — and build it as a [structured deck](#structured-decks) unless the user asks for a quick throwaway |
| **Edit** an existing deck, or build from a template | unzip → edit `ppt/slides/slideN.xml` → zip |
| **Read** content | `markitdown deck.pptx` (one block per slide under `<!-- Slide number: N -->` markers); visual grid: `python scripts/thumbnail.py deck.pptx` |

## Scripts

Paths are relative to this skill's directory. Everything else is plain Python, `node`, or shell.

| Script | What it does |
|---|---|
| `scripts/thumbnail.py deck.pptx [prefix]` | Labeled grid of every slide, for picking template layouts. `.pptx` only. Pass `prefix` — it defaults to `thumbnails`, which overwrites the grids of any other deck done in the same directory |
| `scripts/add_slide.py unpacked/ slide2.xml [--after slideN.xml]` | Duplicate a slide (or a `slideLayoutN.xml`) with all the package bookkeeping. Also takes a `.pptx` directly with `-o out.pptx` |
| `scripts/clean.py unpacked/` | Delete slides, media, and rels no longer referenced. Run **after** `<p:sldIdLst>` is final |
| `scripts/apply_theme.js` | Node module: `const { applyTheme } = require("<this skill's directory>/scripts/apply_theme.js")`. `await applyTheme("deck.pptx", THEME)` after `pres.writeFile()` writes `THEME`'s colors and name (escaped for XML) into the deck's theme, for [structured decks](#structured-decks). Also a CLI: `node scripts/apply_theme.js deck.pptx theme.json` |
| `scripts/office/validate.py deck.pptx [--original src.pptx]` | Schema, relationship, content-type, chart and slide checks; each failure names its fix. Pass `--original` for any template-derived deck — it baselines the schema checks against the template, so the template's own XSD errors don't read as yours |
| `scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf deck.pptx` | LibreOffice wrapper — bare `soffice` hangs in this sandbox |

## Creating with pptxgenjs — gotchas

`pptxgenjs` is preinstalled — do not run `npm install` first; write the script and `require('pptxgenjs')` directly. Only if that require fails: `npm install pptxgenjs`. The model knows the API; these are the footguns:

- **Set `pres.layout` before adding slides.** The default canvas is `LAYOUT_16x9` = **10" × 5.625"**, not 13.3" wide. Coordinates past the edge are written, not clamped — the shape just isn't on the slide. (`LAYOUT_WIDE` is 13.3" × 7.5".)
- **Hex colors: never `#`, never 8 digits.** `color: "FF0000"`. Both `"#FF0000"` and alpha baked into the hex (`"00000020"`) **corrupt the file**. For translucency: `transparency: 0-100` on fills and images, `opacity: 0.0-1.0` on shadows — each is silently ignored on the other.
- **pptxgenjs mutates option objects in place** (converts values to EMU on first use). Never share one `shadow`/options object across two `add*` calls — build a fresh object each time.
- **Shadow `offset` must be ≥ 0** — a negative offset corrupts the file. To cast a shadow upward, use `angle: 270` with a positive offset.
- **`letterSpacing` is silently ignored** — the real option is `charSpacing`.
- **Lists:** `bullet: true` on each item, never a literal `•` (renders double bullets). Set `breakLine: true` on every array item except the last. Space bulleted paragraphs with `paraSpaceAfter`, not `lineSpacing` (huge gaps).
- **One `new pptxgen()` per output file** — never reuse an instance.
- **`rectRadius` only works on `ROUNDED_RECTANGLE`**, not `RECTANGLE`.
- **Gradient fills aren't supported** — use a gradient image as the background instead.
- **Every `addText` call without a `placeholder` needs `isTextBox: true`** — without it the shape lacks `txBox="1"`, so screen readers announce the text as a "graphic" instead of a text box. No visual change.
- **Text boxes have built-in internal padding** — set `margin: 0` whenever text must align with a shape, line, or icon at the same x.
- **Speaker notes go in `slide.addNotes("...")`** (plain text, once per slide), never in a text box on the slide.
- **Keep charts native.** Use `addChart()` for everything PowerPoint can chart (pass an array of `{type, data, options}` for combos). For PowerPoint-native features the library doesn't expose (trendlines, error bars), compute the extra series yourself or post-process the generated OOXML — do not fall back to a rendered image. Only chart types PowerPoint has no native form for (Sankey, network, chord) go in as images.
- **Default charts render bare** — no title, no data labels, dated palette. Set `showTitle` + `title`, `showValue: true` + `dataLabelPosition`, `chartColors: [...]` from your palette, and quiet the frame (`catAxisLabelColor`/`valAxisLabelColor`, `valGridLine: { color, size }`, `catGridLine: { style: "none" }`, `showLegend: false` for a single series).
- **On a stacked bar or column chart, `dataLabelPosition` must be `ctr`, `inEnd`, or `inBase`.** `outEnd` **corrupts the file**.
- **A combo series using `secondaryValAxis`/`secondaryCatAxis` needs both `valAxes` and `catAxes` on the chart options, two entries each.** Without them pptxgenjs writes axis *ids* it never declares, and PowerPoint **discards that chart** and reports the file as corrupt. Supplying only `valAxes` is not enough.
- **After `writeFile()`, run `python scripts/office/validate.py deck.pptx`.** It reports the two chart faults above and the slide-XML defects PowerPoint refuses, and names the fix for each. Fix them in your generator, not by hand-editing the packed XML.
- **Never reorder the children of `<p:presentation>`.** pptxgenjs writes `<p:notesMasterIdLst>` right after `<p:sldIdLst>` and points both masters at one theme part. PowerPoint reads that happily — move the element and the same deck becomes unopenable.
- **Icons:** render `react-icons` to SVG (`ReactDOMServer.renderToStaticMarkup`), rasterize with `sharp` at ≥256px, and insert via `addImage({ data: "image/png;base64," + buf.toString("base64") })` — the `image/png;base64,` prefix is required (`react-icons`, `react`, `react-dom`, and `sharp` are preinstalled — `npm install react-icons react react-dom sharp` only if a require fails).
- **`defineSlideMaster()` creates a slide *layout*, not a master** — one `slideLayoutN.xml` per call, under a single master you cannot change. Call them layouts when talking to the user.
- **`pres.company` and a `defineSlideMaster()` `title` are written into the XML unescaped** — an `&` in either (`"Harrow & Sons"`) leaves `docProps/app.xml` or the layout unparseable, and `validate.py` fails. Write `&` there, and in the matching `masterName`. `title`, `subject`, `author`, section titles, `objectName`, notes and slide text are escaped for you.

### Structured decks

A deck built on a theme, layouts, placeholders and sections can be restyled in one place and edited in PowerPoint without fighting it. Build every new deck this way unless the user asks for a quick throwaway.

1. **Theme first:** `const THEME = { name, headFontFace, bodyFontFace, colors: { dk1, lt1, dk2, lt2, accent1 … accent6, hlink, folHlink } }`, colors in hex. `pres.theme` takes the two fonts and nothing else. Name no font after that — titles get the heading font, other text the body font — except on chart text, which is hard-coded Arial: give its `*FontFace` options `"+mn-lt"` (theme body font; `"+mj-lt"` is the heading font).
2. **`const C = pres.SchemeColor` for every color** — `C.text1`/`C.text2` are `dk1`/`dk2`, `C.background1`/`C.background2` are `lt1`/`lt2`. These take hex only, read from `THEME`: `valGridLine.color`, `catGridLine.color`, `shadow.color`, and on a one-series bar chart `invertedColors` or more than one `chartColors`. A scheme color there is written as `<a:srgbClr val="bg2"/>` without complaint, and being hex, these will not follow a later change of theme.
3. **Sections:** `pres.addSection({ title })` just before that section's first slide, then `sectionTitle` on every `addSlide`. A slide without one — or, when sections are all declared up front, a table's auto-paged continuation slides — lands in a stray "Default-N" section.
4. **One layout per slide frame** (`defineSlideMaster()`): title, section divider, title only, chart + commentary, table; dark and light variants if the design alternates. Text regions are named placeholders carrying position, size, weight and `color` — chart, image and table placeholders need a `color` too, or prompt text and arrays of runs come out hard-coded `000000`. Footer text, logo and `slideNumber` go on the layout, never on a slide.
5. **Fill by name:** `addSlide({ masterName, sectionTitle })`, then `addText("…", { placeholder: "title" })` with no position, size or color — the placeholder's own options win, and anything it doesn't set (italic, `align`, `fontFace`) still applies; style one run with `[{ text, options }]`. A misspelt `placeholder` or `masterName` fails silently (a stray text box at 0,0; the blank layout). Only `title`, `body` and `chart` placeholders fill by name alone: `addImage({ placeholder })` takes the placeholder's x and y but not its size (a 1" × 1" picture) — pass `w`/`h` too. `addTable({ placeholder })` takes its x and y only — always pass `w`; when it auto-pages it ignores the placeholder and runs off the slide, so also pass `x`, `y` and `autoPageSlideStartY` (same as `y`, or continuation pages are laid out from the top margin), give the layout a `margin` whose bottom clears the footer, and fill the continuation slides' titles through `slide.newAutoPagedSlides`.
6. **A layout is the frame, not the "layout" Design Ideas means.** Cards, icons, stat callouts and images are still composed slide by slide on top of it, in scheme colors, each with an `objectName` — every Design Idea applies, and most content slides sit on the title-only layout.
7. **Write, then apply the theme:** `await pres.writeFile({ fileName: "deck.pptx" })`, then `await applyTheme("deck.pptx", THEME)`. pptxgenjs cannot write theme colors: until this runs, scheme colors resolve to Office's stock palette. It throws, changing nothing, on a scheme color in a hex-only option — fix what it names and rebuild.

## Editing existing decks and templates

Pick layouts first: `python scripts/thumbnail.py template.pptx template-thumbs` writes a labeled grid of every slide and prints the file(s) it created — `template-thumbs.jpg`, split into `template-thumbs-N.jpg` past 12 slides. **Always pass that second argument, named after the deck.** It defaults to `thumbnails`, so two decks thumbnailed in one directory silently overwrite each other's grids — the first deck's are simply gone (template analysis only — visual QA needs the full-resolution renders from [Converting to Images](#converting-to-images); it only accepts `.pptx`, so copy a `.potx` to a `.pptx` name first). Use it with `markitdown` to map each content section onto a template slide, and vary the layouts — don't put every section on the same title-and-bullets slide.

```bash
python3 -c "import sys,zipfile; zipfile.ZipFile(sys.argv[1]).extractall('unpacked')" deck.pptx
python scripts/add_slide.py unpacked/ slide2.xml --after slide2.xml   # duplicate a slide (or slideLayoutN.xml); prints the new slide's path
# reorder / delete slides = edit <p:sldIdLst> in ppt/presentation.xml
python scripts/clean.py unpacked/                                     # after deletions: removes orphaned slides, media, rels
# edit slide content in ppt/slides/slideN.xml
(cd unpacked && rm -f ../out.pptx && zip -Xr ../out.pptx .)           # zip from INSIDE the dir; rm first or deleted parts survive
python scripts/office/validate.py out.pptx --original deck.pptx
```

- **Do all structural work — add, delete, reorder — before editing any slide's content.** `add_slide.py` copies a slide file verbatim, so duplicating after you edit clones the edited content; and `clean.py` deletes any slide missing from `<p:sldIdLst>`, including one you just wrote.
- **Never copy a slide file by hand** — `add_slide.py` does every registration a new slide needs and reports what it made (`Created ppt/slides/slide17.xml from slide2.xml`). It also works directly on a file: `add_slide.py deck.pptx slide2.xml -o out.pptx` — **pass `-o`, or it rewrites the input deck in place.** A duplicated slide still *references* its source's chart/SmartArt/embedded-object parts rather than cloning them, so editing one slide's chart changes the other's.
- **If you use `python-pptx`**, three things it won't do: duplicate a slide (its only entry point is `add_slide(layout)`), preserve formatting through `text_frame.text = "..."` (that collapses the paragraph to a single unstyled run — assign `run.text` instead), or read the SVG/EMF most template art uses (`add_picture` raises `UnidentifiedImageError`).
- Legacy `.ppt` must be converted first: `python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pptx file.ppt`. `.potx` templates unpack and pack identically — keep the `.potx` extension on the output.
- To reuse a template icon or image, duplicate a slide or layout that already contains it.

When filling in a template:

- If you script an XML transform, parse with `defusedxml.minidom` — round-tripping OOXML through `xml.etree.ElementTree` rewrites namespace prefixes and corrupts the deck.
- **Template slots ≠ source items.** If the template shows 4 team members and you have 3, delete the 4th member's entire group (image + text boxes), not just its text — then check for orphaned visuals in QA.
- One `<a:p>` per list item — never concatenate items into a single paragraph. Copy the sibling `<a:pPr>` to preserve spacing, and put `b="1"` on the `<a:rPr>` of titles, section headers, and inline labels (`Status:`, `Owner:`).
- Let bullets inherit from the layout; only add `<a:buChar>`, `<a:buAutoNum>` (numbered), or `<a:buNone>` to override — never a literal `•` in the text.
- Text with leading or trailing spaces needs `xml:space="preserve"` on its `<a:t>`.

## Deck content and flow

- **One message per slide.** A deck goes theme by theme, message by message.
- **A common structure is the pyramid:** the main message up front, an executive summary that previews the sections, the sections themselves, then a conclusion, usually with next steps that act on the findings.
- **Match the structure to the size of the deck.** A short deck might not need an introduction and a conclusion; a long deck might need dividers between topics.
- **Build toward what the deck is for:** a decision, consensus, a celebration, resolving a disagreement, or opening a discussion.
- **Build for how it will be used.** A live deck gets narration and possibly discussion; a pre-read has to carry the whole narrative itself. An executive audience in a live meeting needs few words and highly visual slides. Detailed, word-heavy slides are sometimes right for subject-matter experts or for a deck read offline. Analytical reports lean on charts and tables.
- **Size a live deck to the talk:** about 1.5 to 2 minutes per slide, with time left for questions if there will be any.

## Design Ideas

**Don't create boring slides.** Plain bullets on a white background won't impress anyone. Consider ideas from this list for each slide.

### Before Starting

- **Pick a bold, content-informed color palette**: The palette should feel designed for THIS topic. If swapping your colors into a completely different presentation would still "work," you haven't made specific enough choices.
- **Dominance over equality**: One color should dominate (60-70% visual weight), with 1-2 supporting tones and one sharp accent. Never give all colors equal weight.
- **Dark/light contrast**: Dark backgrounds for title + conclusion slides, light for content ("sandwich" structure). Or commit to dark throughout for a premium feel.
- **Commit to a visual motif**: Pick ONE distinctive element and repeat it — rounded image frames, icons in colored circles. Carry it across every slide. **Do not use a color bar or accent stripe as your motif** (see Avoid list).

### Color Palettes

Choose colors that match your topic — don't default to generic blue. Use these palettes as inspiration:

| Theme | Primary | Secondary | Accent |
|-------|---------|-----------|--------|
| **Midnight Executive** | `1E2761` (navy) | `CADCFC` (ice blue) | `FFFFFF` (white) |
| **Forest & Moss** | `2C5F2D` (forest) | `97BC62` (moss) | `F5F5F5` (cream) |
| **Coral Energy** | `F96167` (coral) | `F9E795` (gold) | `2F3C7E` (navy) |
| **Warm Terracotta** | `B85042` (terracotta) | `E7E8D1` (sand) | `A7BEAE` (sage) |
| **Ocean Gradient** | `065A82` (deep blue) | `1C7293` (teal) | `21295C` (midnight) |
| **Charcoal Minimal** | `36454F` (charcoal) | `F2F2F2` (off-white) | `212121` (black) |
| **Teal Trust** | `028090` (teal) | `00A896` (seafoam) | `02C39A` (mint) |
| **Berry & Cream** | `6D2E46` (berry) | `A26769` (dusty rose) | `ECE2D0` (cream) |
| **Sage Calm** | `84B59F` (sage) | `69A297` (eucalyptus) | `50808E` (slate) |
| **Cherry Bold** | `990011` (cherry) | `FCF6F5` (off-white) | `2F3C7E` (navy) |

### For Each Slide

**Every slide needs a visual element** — image, chart, icon, or shape. Text-only slides are forgettable.

**Layout options:**
- Two-column (text left, illustration on right)
- Icon + text rows (icon in colored circle, bold header, description below)
- 2x2 or 2x3 grid (image on one side, grid of content blocks on other)
- Half-bleed image (full left or right side) with content overlay

**Data display:**
- Large stat callouts (big numbers 60-72pt with small labels below)
- Comparison columns (before/after, pros/cons, side-by-side options)
- Timeline or process flow (numbered steps, arrows)

**Visual polish:**
- Icons in small colored circles next to section headers
- Italic accent text for key stats or taglines

### Typography

**Font names you write into the .pptx are rendered by the user's PowerPoint, not by this environment.** Your visual QA renders via LibreOffice, which substitutes fonts it doesn't have — and for some fonts the substitute has different widths, so your QA preview can show text overflow (or fit) that the real deck won't have. To keep your QA trustworthy:

- **Safe fonts** (render true-to-width in QA *and* ship with Office): **Arial, Calibri, Cambria, Times New Roman, Courier New, Bookman Old Style, Century Schoolbook**. Use these for body text and anything where fit matters.
- **Headers with personality at zero QA risk**: pair a safe-list serif header (Cambria, Bookman Old Style, Century Schoolbook) with a safe-list sans body (Calibri or Arial). You get visual contrast without giving up reliable overflow checks.
- **If the user asks for a font outside the safe list** (e.g. Georgia or Trebuchet MS): use it where the user asked, but size those containers with extra slack (~10%) and don't trust QA text-fit on those elements — the preview of that font is approximate. If the user hasn't specified, prefer safe-list fonts for body text.
- **QA-unreliable fonts** (substitute has different widths — overflow checks can be wrong): Georgia, Trebuchet MS, Impact, Arial Black, Garamond, Consolas, Palatino Linotype. Calibri Light substitution varies by environment; treat as QA-unreliable. Fine for titles/accents with slack; don't trust QA text-fit on these.
- **Never default to Aptos** — Office's post-2023 default has no metric-compatible substitute here *and* is missing from older Office installs, so it's unreliable on both ends.

| Element | Size |
|---------|------|
| Slide title | 36-44pt bold |
| Section header | 20-24pt bold |
| Body text | 14-16pt |
| Captions | 10-12pt muted |

### Spacing

- 0.5" minimum margins
- 0.3-0.5" between content blocks
- Leave breathing room—don't fill every inch

### Avoid (Common Mistakes)

- **Don't repeat the same layout** — vary columns, cards, and callouts across slides
- **Don't end a slide title with a period**
- **Don't let titles drift between slides of the same type** — content slides with the title at the top put it at the same position, font, size, and alignment on every slide; a different slide type (a section divider with the title mid-slide) can place it differently
- **Don't change how chart labels look from chart to chart** — axis and data labels use the same color, font, and size on every chart in the deck; vary one only where a chart needs it (a second axis, a highlighted series, a label sitting on a dark bar)
- **Don't center body text** — left-align paragraphs and lists; center only titles
- **Don't skimp on size contrast** — titles need 36pt+ to stand out from 14-16pt body
- **Don't default to blue** — pick colors that reflect the specific topic
- **Don't mix spacing randomly** — choose 0.3" or 0.5" gaps and use consistently
- **Don't style one slide and leave the rest plain** — commit fully or keep it simple throughout
- **Don't create text-only slides** — add images, icons, charts, or visual elements; avoid plain title + bullets
- **Don't forget text box padding** — when aligning lines or shapes with text edges, set `margin: 0` on the text box or offset the shape to account for padding
- **Don't use low-contrast elements** — icons AND text need strong contrast against the background; avoid light text on light backgrounds or dark text on dark backgrounds
- **NEVER use accent lines under titles** — these are a hallmark of AI-generated slides; use whitespace or background color instead
- **NEVER add decorative color bars or accent stripes** — this includes: header/footer bars spanning the slide width, vertical sidebar stripes down one edge of the slide, thin accent stripes along one edge of a card or content block, and "single-side borders" on rectangles. These read as AI-generated filler. If you want to set a card apart, use a subtle background tint, a drop shadow, or an icon — not an edge stripe.
- **Don't default to cream/beige backgrounds** — when no background is specified, use white (`FFFFFF`) or the user's brand palette; avoid warm-neutral defaults like `F5F5DC`, `FAF0E6`, `FAEBD7`, `FFF8E1`
- **Don't ship text that overflows its shape** — if text doesn't fit, reduce font size, split across slides, or enlarge the container; never leave content cut off or spilling past bounds. **Don't shrink below the sizes in the Typography table** (body text 14pt, captions 10pt) in a deck you create — once you reach that floor, cut words, enlarge the container, or split the slide instead; when editing an existing deck or template, match its sizes

## QA (Required)

Your first render usually has a few real issues — overlaps, overflow, misalignment. Find and fix those, re-render only the slides you changed, and stop.

### Content QA (required)

```bash
markitdown output.pptx
```

Check for missing content, typos, wrong order.

**When using templates, check for leftover placeholder text:**

```bash
markitdown output.pptx | grep -iE "\bx{3,}\b|lorem|ipsum|\bTODO|\[insert|this.*(page|slide).*layout"
```

If grep returns results, fix them before declaring success.

### File QA (required)

```bash
python scripts/office/validate.py output.pptx                      # built from scratch
python scripts/office/validate.py output.pptx --original src.pptx  # built from a template
```

**If the deck came from a template, always pass `--original`.** A template may itself
contain parts the XSD rejects, so a bare run can report failures you never caused — and
a genuine regression can hide among them. `--original` baselines
the schema and slide checks against the template, suppressing errors it already had.
The structural checks — relationships, content types, charts — ignore `--original` and
report template-inherited problems either way, so read those on their own merits.

pptxgenjs emits chart XML PowerPoint refuses to open, and every other tool
accepts: python-pptx opens those decks, LibreOffice renders them, the XSD
passes them. Every failure names its fix. Fix it in the generator and rebuild.

### Visual QA (required)

Convert the slides to images (see [Converting to Images](#converting-to-images)) and inspect every one. After staring at the generating code you tend to see what you expect rather than what rendered, so look at the images fresh (a subagent works well for this if you have one). User-visible defects to look for:

- **Text overflow or text cut off at a box or slide boundary — check this first.** It is the most common defect and always user-visible. (For a font the previewer renders unreliably per Typography, the preview is approximate: trust the ~10% slack you left, not its apparent fit.)
- Overlapping elements (text through shapes, lines through words, stacked elements)
- Source citations or footers colliding with content above
- Elements too close (< 0.3" gaps) or cards/sections nearly touching
- Uneven gaps (large empty area in one place, cramped in another)
- Insufficient margin from slide edges (< 0.5")
- Columns or similar elements not aligned consistently
- Low-contrast text (e.g., light gray text on cream-colored background)
- Template decoration mispositioned after text replacement — e.g., a title underline positioned for one line, but the replaced title wrapped to two
- Low-contrast icons (e.g., dark icons on dark backgrounds without a contrasting circle)
- Text boxes too narrow causing excessive wrapping
- Titles at different heights, or chart labels that look different from chart to chart, across slides of the same type — compare slides with each other, not only each slide with itself
- A word or number broken across two lines — a word split mid-word, or a figure separated from its unit ("26" on one line, "M" on the next)
- Leftover placeholder content

## Converting to Images

Convert presentations to individual slide images for visual inspection:

```bash
python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf output.pptx
rm -f slide-*.jpg
pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 output.pdf slide
ls -1 "$PWD"/slide-*.jpg
```

**Pass the absolute paths printed above directly to the view tool.** The `rm` clears stale images from prior runs. `pdftoppm` zero-pads based on page count: `slide-1.jpg` for decks under 10 pages, `slide-01.jpg` for 10-99, `slide-001.jpg` for 100+.

**After fixes, rerun all four commands above** — the PDF must be regenerated from the edited `.pptx` before `pdftoppm` can reflect your changes.
